16,24: Patroclus kept steering his horses toward wherever he saw the most men fleeing in confusion, cheering on his men as he went. Chariots were being smashed in all directions, and many a man tumbled from his own car and fell beneath the wheels of Patroclus’s chariot. Its immortal horses, which the gods had given to Peleus, sprang over the trench in a single bound as they raced on. Patroclus was set on getting near Hector, for he had his heart fixed on spearing him, but Hector’s horses were now hurrying him away. As the whole dark earth bows before a tempest on an autumn day, when Zeus rains his hardest to punish men who give crooked judgments in their courts, drive justice out of them and ignore the decrees of heaven, and all the rivers run full, and the torrents tear many a new channel as they roar headlong from the mountains to the dark sea, and it goes badly for the works of men, so great was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses in their flight.
22,29: So the head of Hector was dishonored in the dust. His mother tore her hair and flung her veil away with a loud cry when she saw her son. His father groaned piteously, and all through the city the people began to weep and wail. It was as if the whole of frowning Ilium were smoldering in fire. The people could hardly hold Priam back, so hot was his haste to rush out of the city gates. He groveled in the mire and begged them, calling each one by name. “Let me be, my friends,” he cried, “and for all your sorrow, allow me to go alone to the ships of the Achaeans. Let me plead with this cruel and terrible man. Perhaps he will respect the feelings of his fellow men and have pity on my old age. His own father is just such another as I am—Peleus, who bred him and raised him to be the bane of us Trojans, and of me more than of all others. He has killed many a son of mine in the flower of his youth. Yet however I grieve for those, I grieve for one—Hector—more than for them all, and the bitterness of my sorrow will bring me down to the house of Hades. I wish he had died in my arms. Then both his ill-starred mother who bore him and I would have had the comfort of weeping and mourning over him.”
16,8: Meanwhile Achilles went everywhere among the tents and told his Myrmidons to put on their armor. As fierce, ravening wolves feast on a horned stag they have killed in the mountains, their jaws red with blood, and then go in a pack to lap water from a clear spring with their long thin tongues, reeking of blood and slaughter and knowing no fear because hunger drives them, so the leaders and counselors of the Myrmidons gathered around the good squire of the swift descendant of Aeacus, and Achilles himself stood among them, urging on both men and horses.
16,12: In front of them all, two men armed themselves—Patroclus and Automedon—two men with one mind, to lead the Myrmidons. Then Achilles went into his tent and opened the lid of the strong chest that silver-footed Thetis had given him to take on board ship, and had filled with shirts, cloaks against the cold, and good thick rugs. In this chest he kept a cup of rare workmanship. No man but himself might drink from it, and he made offerings from it to no god except father Zeus. He took the cup from the chest and cleansed it with sulphur. Then he rinsed it in clean water, washed his hands, and drew wine. He stood in the middle of the court and prayed, looking toward heaven and pouring out the wine as a drink offering. Zeus, whose joy is in thunder, did not fail to see him. “King Zeus,” he cried, “lord of Dodona, god of the Pelasgi, you who live far away and rule wintry Dodona, where your prophets the Selli live around you with unwashed feet and beds made on the ground—if you heard me when I prayed to you before, and honored me by sending disaster on the Achaeans, grant me now the fulfillment of one more prayer. I will stay here where my ships are lying, but I am sending my comrade into battle at the head of many Myrmidons. Grant, all-seeing Zeus, that victory goes with him. Put your courage into his heart, so that Hector learns whether my squire is man enough to fight alone, or whether his might is unbeatable only when I myself enter the turmoil of war. Afterward, when he has driven the fighting and the battle cry away from the ships, grant that he returns unharmed, with his armor and his comrades, fighters in close combat.”
24,41: The old man was afraid of him and obeyed. Then the son of Peleus sprang out through the door of his house like a lion. He did not go alone. His two squires, Automedon and Alcimus, went with him. Now that Patroclus was dead, he valued these two above all his other comrades. They unyoked the horses and mules, and told Priam’s herald and attendant to sit inside the house. They lifted the ransom for Hector’s body down from the wagon, but left two mantles and a fine shirt for Achilles to wrap the body in when it was given back to be taken home. Then Achilles called to his servants and told them to wash the body and anoint it. First he took it to a place where Priam could not see it. He was afraid that Priam, seeing it, might break out in the bitterness of his grief and enrage him, so that he would kill the old man and sin against the word of Zeus. When the servants had washed and anointed the body and wrapped it in a fair shirt and mantle, Achilles himself lifted it onto a bier, and he and his men laid it on the wagon. As he did so he cried aloud and called on his dear comrade by name. “Do not be angry with me, Patroclus,” he said, “if you learn, even in the house of Hades, that I gave Hector back to his father for a ransom. It was not an unworthy one, and I will share it with you fairly.”
